name: Flag
lede: Flag is a dark, grayish purplish blue from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, first recorded in 1918 and closest to navy among the core colors.

sections.title: A 1918 name, no documented origin
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary lists Flag on plate 46, swatch I12, first recorded in 1918 [1]. The book gives no reason for the name, and whether it refers to a national flag, a flagstone, or the flag-shaped iris flower is undocumented here [1]. The same plate carries two close neighbors, Grape Blue and Roma Blue, both first recorded nearly a decade later, in 1927 and 1928 [1]. Our own classification places the hue in the ISCC-NBS region called grayish purplish blue, Munsell notation 7.8PB 2.5/3.9 [2].

The nearest named colors on file are [[colonial]], [[bramble]], [[dark-bluish-violet]] and [[dusky-blue]], at 2.8, 3.7, 3.8 and 4 ΔE [2]. Flag reads more purple and less black than true [[navy]], and sits near [[blue]] and [[purple]] on the same dark axis [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of Flag covers at least five percent of the canvas in 90 of them, about 0.4 percent overall, as photographed [3]. Use spikes in the 1910s, over six times the archive's average rate for that decade, driven in part by Henri Matisse, who carries it in 4 of his 50 archived paintings, over twenty times the average rate [3]. Its single strongest companion word is Navy, at over eighty times the average co-occurrence [3]. These counts read photographs of varnished paintings, not pigments [3].

origin.named_after: undocumented; possibly a flag, a flagstone, or the flag iris, but the dictionary does not say
origin.source: Maerz and Paul, A Dictionary of Color

questions.q: True or false: Maerz and Paul explain where the name Flag comes from.
Which painter uses Flag at over twenty times the archive's average rate?

openers: Flag's origin is undocumented, but it spikes in the 1910s, largely through Henri Matisse, who used it over twenty times the archive's average rate.
